about: The Country and the city's loop (Docs/Design/68-the-country-and-the-city-loop.md). The Country stands for the farms, mines, woods and villages beyond the walls until they are built: what a keeper draws from the store room is bought from it (its purse is the account outside:<market id>), and every day it spends what it took in on the city's goods, keeping a reserve. `markets` is a list so that the smaller towns can each become a market with its own purse and basket later; there is one for now. A market's `basket` is what its people buy in the city, as shares of its day's spending (any whole numbers; they are scaled to the money it has), weighted toward the trades with time to spare (tools/city_loop.py checks it against the city's makers). `wages` says who pays a post that is neither a shop's keeper nor its hand (those are paid by their shop's till) nor the watch (the treasury): the first rule with a word in the post's title, in lower case. `food` and `comforts` are the residents' buying. The numbers are placeholders; the per-world settings (on and off, the reserve, the toll, the wages, carriage, goods the Country no longer supplies) are the world's own, in live.economy and Atlas's Economy page.

markets.name: the Country
markets.people: the country folk not yet placed (Docs/Design/66-worlds-atlas-and-dm.md, 2): when they are given farms, their farms take over the goods they grow

rules.name: the Crown's and the offices' heads
rules.about: The heads of the Crown's household and of the city's offices (doc 68, Progress, "First fixes"): the Queen, the King's daughter, the City Office's head; and ("Trades": the user, 2026-10-31, office heads get a head's pay) the King, the two chancellors, the royal secretary, the Crown's treasurer, the magistrate, the keeper of the rolls (the Records Office), the collector of customs, the warden of the Market Hall, the abbot, the keepers of the Washhouse and the Bathhouse, and the Watch's commander (a guard: the watch's post, at this wage). Paid by the treasury at a keeper's wage (a head's), not a clerk's.

rules.name: the Houses' heads
rules.about: The Minor Houses' family members who run a House's own affairs (doc 68, Progress, "First fixes"): a House's lending, the Grayrock wharf; and the heads of the Houses' offices ("Trades"): the harbourmaster of the Wharf Office, the Counting House's overseer. Kept by their House's estates in the Country (as the Houses' other people), at a keeper's wage.

rules.name: the sea trade
rules.about: Carriage by sea and the Country's warehouses: the ships' unloading, the cranes, the carrying up from the wharf, the stores' tallies.

rules.name: the Houses' people
rules.about: The Great and Minor Houses' people, kept by their estates in the Country: heads, stewards, servants, the Houses' own trades.

rules.name: public posts
rules.about: Public posts: the Crown and the Council, the courts, the offices, the Records Office, the customs, the lamps, the markets' hands, the washhouse and baths, the teachers, the abbey, the cathedral and the chapels.

estates.about: The Houses' estates (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, Phase 6; the rule `estates`, 1, on): each House's own purse, which collects its lands' rents (the works' surplus and the food farms' land rents, by their `house`; the country workshops' share, by theirs) and pays its own people first, keeping countryPostsDays nights of their wages and its share of the Country's reserve (by its posts' wages) before it buys the Country's basket (the realm's trade beyond it, through the wharf), its House's tables' luxuries and its patrons' work. A Country post (a `wages` rule with payer `country`) is the first estate's whose `words` are in its label, in lower case, else the first whose words are in its workplace's cell id, else the one that `grants`. `fund` `country`: the estate is the Country's own purse (outside:country): Grayrock runs the wharf (doc 67, R28), so the sea trade's takings (the ships' goods, the iron and the lime sold through the store room), the basket and the arrivals stay in it; the others are estate:<id>. The estate that `grants` (the Crown's: its land rents are the realm's grain, herds and salt) keeps the posts no other estate's words match (the Minor Houses, who hold no land in the realm, and the Harrowgates of the King's household) and, each night before the wages, gives any estate short of tonight's posts what it lacks, from what it holds over its own (a grant, the Crown's levy on the realm's land; recorded, never the treasury's). Before its grants it levies the other estates (after estates6, whose Crown granted only yesterday's land rents while the wharf held two nights of its posts and more): what they hold over their own keep, up to what it lacks of its own (its posts' nights and the others' lacks), then, still short of tonight's posts and grants, what they hold over tonight's posts; so every post is paid whenever the estates together hold tonight's. An estate buys only with what it holds over its keep and never more than the estates together hold over the one purse's keep (the reserve and countryPostsDays nights of all their posts), and the Houses' tables together take at most rules.luxuryHousesMost pieces a day. With the rule off every House's money and post is the Country's one purse again, as before Phase 6 (an estate's purse is emptied into it that night); switched on, the Country's money is shared between the estates by their posts' wages.

list.name: House Grayrock's estate (the wharf and the sea trade)

food.about: Each household goes to market once a day at its own hour, and tops every member up to `days` days of food; one still short of `shortDays` tries again each hour until the shops shut. Food is picked among what the open shops have, the better the nourishment for the price the likelier. Whoever in the household has the money pays.

comforts.about: A household holding more than `above` pennies a head spends `share` of what is over it a day on comforts from the city's shops, used up at once: the better-off buy drink, candles, cloth and treats, so that savings come back to the shops. (Doc 68, Progress, "First fixes": 40p and a fifth, as set 2 measured; at most `rules.comfortsMost` purchases a day.) The day's budget pays for the city's services first (`services`), then comforts.

luxuries.about: The luxuries (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, Phase 5; the user's decision, 2026-11-03: cheese becomes a comic luxury for wolves, highly desired by all, its price allowed to climb to meet demand so that mostly the rich and noble afford it, but no wolf breaks the bank for it). A luxury is never bought as food. Each household, at its market hour after its food and its needs (the fuel among them; the city's households pay no rent), wants one a head (rules.luxuryMost), bought only from what it holds over its keep, at most rules.luxuryShare percent of that a day: a household of the Houses (by its class) keeps `comforts.above` pennies a head, any other rules.luxuryAbove (after country5, doc 72: the middle class bought nearly all of it, the Houses' wolves holding no more a head than they). The Houses' own tables: once a day the Country's purse (the Houses' estates) buys luxuries with rules.luxuryHouses percent of what it holds over its reserve and its posts' nights, at most rules.luxuryHousesMost pieces, at the shops' own price, before its basket. So the rich and the noble are its buyers; each piece at its shop's own price: a shop's price for a luxury follows its stock as every ware's does (rules.stockPrices) but in its own band, up to rules.luxuryPriceBand percent over the season's price, by rules.luxuryPriceStep thousandths a day, and outside the city's price level (its climb never cheapens the rest). The luxuries' budget comes before the comforts' (out of the same money).

rules.about: The loop's rules the DM can tune (Docs/Design/68-the-country-and-the-city-loop.md, Progress, "First fixes"; each world's own in live.economy.rules, migration 0058, the DM's Economy tab and Atlas's Economy page). comfortsMost: the most comforts a household buys a day (it was 20, which kept the rich from spending their savings). almsADay: pennies a head the city's alms make a household up to after the day's wages (was 7: a day's food with nothing over for a Restday). treasuryCap: pennies the treasury keeps; what it holds over this at 18:00, after its own posts, pays what the shops' tills could not pay their posts (wageSupport percent of each till's shortfall; each post the same share of its wage). workBankHours: the crew's hours a shop may bank for a long craft, in hours of the whole crew's work; 0 (the default): as long as the business's longest craft and an hour more (at least two), so a lone cartographer can make a map over two days (was 2, which no 13.9-hour map could fit). fairFood: 1 = at market the members with least food buy first, everyone to `food.shortDays` before anyone to `food.days`, and only foods some member can pay for are picked; 0 = the old order. services: 1 = households buy the city's services (`services`) from their comforts budget; 0 = none. servicesCityShare: the percent of each service's price that goes to the treasury (the city); the rest stays in the shop's till. Trades and the follow-ups (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"): suppliers: 1 = a keeper buys its craft inputs from the city's makers first (`suppliers`: the cooper's casks for the wine makers), at their price, till to till; 0 = all from the store room. patrons: 1 = the trades' patrons (`patrons`: the treasury, the Houses' estates, the wharf) pay for their units' work (the services `for: patrons`) and the armoury's new kit; 0 = none. armourEvery: days between new pieces of kit for each armed wolf. buyAheadDays: days of food more a household buys the day before a Restday or festival (0: none). floatDrawDays: a till's working float, kept back before its wages and its keeper's profit, is its mean draws a day over this many days (1: yesterday's, as it was). floatWagesDays: days of its posts' wages a till keeps over its float before profit (7, a week, as it was). workshopWagesDays (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, after country5): a country workshop's, before what is over goes to its House's estate (4 since country6a: Larkfield's smithy, whose float is a day's iron bars, was still short on some Restdays, 98.0% paid; 3 since country5b's carry-overs, with 2 it was short on most; 2 as the works keep floatDays, and the week of floatWagesDays before that). workshopWageMost (doc 72, after country6a): the most pennies a country workshop's wages drift over the world's (its House takes the profit, but the drift, judged on that share, had raised its crews' wages ~130p a day over their base and left the House, the Country's purse, little): 2, a keeper 16p and a hand 10p at most, the works' and the farms' fixed wages; down as any till's. subsidyToNeed: 1 = the carriage subsidy gives the carters only what their till lacks of tonight's wages and its float (nothing to their keeper's profit); 0 = a quarter of all carriage, as it was. countryPostsDays (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, Phase 3): the nights of its posts' wages the Country keeps in its purse, over its reserve, before its basket and its patrons buy (2: tonight's and the next's, so a run of lean days never leaves its posts unpaid; it was 1). estates (doc 72, Phase 6): 1 = each House its own estate purse (`estates`): its lands' rents in, its people's wages out, the Crown's grants to an estate short of its posts; 0 = the Country's one purse for them all, as before. landRent (doc 72, open question 2, after country3 showed the Country's intake under its posts): the percent of a food farm's takings it pays each night to the House whose land it is on (into the Country's purse, "the Houses' estates and the sea trade", booked by House: Fell the orchards, vines and hives, Grayrock the fishing, the Crown the grain, herds and salt), after its crew's wages and out of what is over its float, the share its basket would have spent (a farm short of its wages pays none); 16 for every food area without its own: landRentFish 9, landRentFruit 4, landRentGrain 28, landRentSalt 8 (each about half its thinnest farm's margin over its wages in its leanest season of country3's year 3; 0: none); a farm with its own `landRent` in country_farms.json pays that rule instead: landRentDairy 32, the three cattle and dairy farms (doc 72, Phase 4: their margin 67-70% of their takings in country3c's year 3, the pig farms' 41% beside them in the meat area; 24 kept the Country 10% over its posts in its leanest season even if Phase 4 took the 187p a day the doc first put on it; 32 after country5, their margin 68-72% after wages and the Country's summer 8.4% over its posts once the workshops took its sales). The treasury's surplus (doc 68, Progress, "The treasury's surplus: works and alms"): surplus: 1 = at 18:00, last (after the treasury's posts, the short tills' wages and the alms), what the treasury holds over treasuryCap and surplusKeep goes back out; 0 = it stays. surplusKeep: pennies over the cap the treasury keeps for the lean seasons (the toll falls in summer and autumn, below its posts and alms). surplusWorks: percent of the surplus to public works orders from the city's trades (`works`), till to till at the catalogue's price. surplusAlms: percent of it to the poorest households, per head, poorest first, up to surplusAlmsTo pennies a head; what one can't place goes to the other, and what neither places stays. The self-correcting rules (doc 68, Progress, "Self-correcting rules"; each gentle, each its switch; what each has drifted to is saved with the society and shown, read only, beside the rules): stockPrices: 1 = a shop's price for a ware follows its stock, up stockPriceStep thousandths a day when it sells out, down as much when more than three days of the day's sales are left over its starting stock (the season's stock-up allowed for), else a quarter step back toward the catalogue's; then the day's factors are scaled so their mean, weighted by sales, is 1 (what is scarce dearer against what is plentiful, the city's prices as a whole the catalogue's); within stockPriceBand percent of the catalogue's (the season's) price, and never under what the store room charges the shop for the ware and a twentieth; on top of the season's price, paid as it is; players pay it too (and a shop offers them SellBackShare of it), the Country's purchases stay at the catalogue's. shelfFollow: 1 = a ware's shelf is shelfCover percent of its sales a day smoothed over about shelfDays days, never under its starting stock; a day it sells out having sold at least its shelf counts as shelfGrow percent more than its shelf (at most 1,000), so a shelf too small to show its demand grows; a Restday's or festival's few sales never lower it; 0 = a quarter more than yesterday's sales, as it was. wageDrift: 1 = every wageDriftDays days a till that paid all its posts every day, its keeper's profit at least wageDriftSpare percent of their wages, raises each post's wage a penny, and one short on more than half of them lowers it a penny, never under wageDriftFloor pennies (a day's food) and at most wageDriftMost either way on a keeper's wage, wageDriftHandMost on a hand's (12 each, from 6: doc 68, Progress, "Players in the shifting market; wider wages; the long runs"); the treasury's and the Country's posts keep their wages. treasuryDrift: 1 = the treasury's level, a slow mean of it at 18:00 over about treasuryDays days, is judged every treasuryJudgeDays days (28; it was a fortnight) against treasuryTarget (5,500p, about where it settles; it was 5,000p: doc 68, Progress, "Births follow deaths; arrivals from the Country; the treasury's target"): over it and treasuryBand percent and not falling, the gate toll eases tollStep tenths of a point and the alms rise a penny a head; under it and not rising, the toll firms and the alms tighten; first judged once the level has had treasuryDays to settle; the toll at most tollDriftMost points from the world's, the alms up to almsDriftMost pennies over almsADay and never under it (the line under hunger). The surplus stays the nightly ceiling; this is the slow trim under it. landRentThin (doc 72, Phase 5, country4's carry-over): the land rent of the thinnest farms (country_farms.json `landRent` "thin": the two lake boats, the two salt works, orchards 2, 4 and 5, 5-8p a day over their wages and rent in country4's year 3, orchard_5 short two nights), 0: none. The luxuries (doc 72, Phase 5, the user's decision; `luxuries`): luxuryShare, the most percent of what a household holds over its keep a head that it spends on luxuries a day, after its food and needs; luxuryMost, the most pieces a head a day; luxuryAbove (after country5: the middle class bought 11.5 a day, the Houses' wolves 0.1, both holding ~50p a head), the keep a head of a household not of the Houses, by its class (the Houses' households keep comforts.above); luxuryHouses, the percent of what the Country's purse holds over its reserve and its posts' nights that it spends a day on luxuries for the Houses' own tables (its basket's money, before the basket), at the shops' own price, at most luxuryHousesMost pieces a day; luxuryPriceBand, how far over the season's price a shop's price for a luxury may climb, in percent (700: eight times; it was 300); luxuryPriceStep, thousandths a day it climbs when the shop sells out (and falls on a glut, a quarter of it back toward the season's on a quiet day).

services.about: The city's services (the user, 2026-10-31: "Make them public services that NPC's have the occasional need to purchase from, but make it items that NPC's buy when they have excess money that isn't needed for other things. The money goes partly to the shop owner and to the city."). Each is a catalogue item (category service, items.json: its name and its price) a business does for a household: bought only from the household's comforts budget (what is over `comforts.above` a head, after food, needs and their reserve), at its market hour, about once every `every` days (a fixed roll of the household and the day: nothing saved), from an open shop of `business` in its community (else anywhere open). Done at once: nothing is kept on a shelf or at home. Of its price `rules.servicesCityShare` percent goes to the treasury, the rest to the shop's till. Each world may turn one off or change its price and frequency (live.economy.services). A service `for: patrons` (doc 68, Progress, "Trades") is never a household's: it is done for each unit of its business's patrons (`patrons`: an armed wolf, a hull, a building) about once every `every` days, paid by the patron, with no city share.

suppliers.about: The city's makers that supply another business's craft inputs first (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"; the rule suppliers): what a `buyer`'s keeper draws for its crafts it buys from a `seller`'s till holding it, at the seller's price (the catalogue's, a dearer season's after), till to till inside the walls (no toll, no carriage), and from the store room only what the city's sellers lack. `goods`: the goods it covers (none: every input the seller sells). A good a shop sells on (doc 72, Phase 5: the resale path) is bought the same way, from the city's makers and the country workshops first, but at the store room's price for it (resaleMarkup of the season's, so the reseller's costs never rise; `price`, a percent of the catalogue's, where a maker would sell under its inputs' cost at that: the smiths' nails and cookpots and the bandages at the catalogue's). The wine makers' casks from the cooper (wine by the cask: crafts.json); and since doc 72's Phase 4 (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, 4.5) the craft inputs the Country's store sold the city's makers: linen cloth from the weaver (its flax from the grain farms), iron hoops from the smithies and the cooperage, planks from the Timberland Sawmill, cord from the chandlery (its hemp from the grain farms), paper from the papermill and the scriptorium, leather from the tannery, ink from the scriptorium and the printing house. A maker's own input (the chandlery's cord for its candles) stays the store room's, but for the ropewalk's (after country5b, doc 72: the ropewalk makes cord too, crafts.json, and sells it the chandleries, the soapworks, the general stores, the jeweller, the tinker and the fletcher; the builders' works and the carpenters sell their planks beside the sawmill: the Country still sold ~26 cord and ~2 planks a day while the ropewalk and the builders' works stood idle on the wage support). Phase 5 (doc 72, 4.6, the country workshops, Data/Economy/workshops.json): Coldwater's soap boiler and chandler (fine soap for the general stores, its cord from the chandlery and the ropewalk), its wool weavers (scarves for the rag-and-bone men), Larkfield's linen weavers (linen beside the city's weaver, and for the presses), the presses and paper mills of Larkfield and Oakhaven (pamphlets for the general stores, paper for the printing house and the cartographer, their ink from the scriptorium and the printing house), the potteries of Fenshore and Southmeadow (clay pots), Larkfield's village smithy (hoops beside the smithies and the cooperage; nails and cookpots); and the doc's leftovers from the city's makers: the general store's and the builders' yard's nails, the rag-and-bone man's and the pawnbroker's cookpots, the barber's bandages. Later chains, such as the mill's flour for the bakers, are a line here.

patrons.about: The trades whose customers are the city, the Houses and the wharf rather than households (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"; the user, 2026-10-31, on the armoury: "Armory should have houses and city as customers ... high cost items replaced occasionally, but repaired frequently which should be the main source of their business"; and the follow-ups: the shipwright's hulls for the wharf and sea carriage, the builders' yard's upkeep of the public buildings and the Houses' halls). Each group is a patron with its units: the posts of `roles` (the watch: every guard's post), else `units` (not placed: a number); `payer` the treasury or a market's id (the Houses' estates and the wharf are the Country, as with the Houses' wages). Once a day, at the first hour one of the trade's shops is open, each unit has each of the trade's services `for: patrons` done about once every `every` days (their prices and frequencies: `services`, the DM's), and where the trade has `pieces`, a new piece bought about once every rules.armourEvery days (one of these the shop holds, at the catalogue's price). A payer spends only what it can spare: the treasury over its float and tonight's posts, the Country over its reserve and its posts.

groups.name: the Houses' armed retainers (their estates: none placed yet, a number)
the wharf's and sea carriage's hulls (the Country)
the Houses' halls (their estates, the Country)

works.about: The city's public works (doc 68, Progress, "The treasury's surplus: works and alms"; the user, 2026-10-31): with its surplus (rules.surplus, surplusWorks) the treasury buys upkeep and goods for the public buildings and services from the city's businesses, at their (the catalogue's) price, till to till. Each trade has `weight` shares of the day's orders (of what is left: what one can't place goes on to the next), spread so that the money becomes wages rather than one owner's profit: a trade's tills with most room under their keeper's profit (their float and a week of their posts' wages) first. `goods`: a service (the builders' yard's work on the public buildings) is done at once; a good comes off the shop's shelves (one left for its customers) and is used up in the works, so the shop makes more.

shelves.about: Dear goods a shop keeps fewer of on its shelves than the usual four (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"): theriac, the apothecary's rare cure-all, one at a time.

seasons.about: The seasons in the Country's supply (Docs/Design/68-the-country-and-the-city-loop.md, Progress, "Seasons and the DM's rules"): each group's goods, and for Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter (the value at each season's middle day; the days between blend in a straight line), in percent of normal: `supply`, how much the Country can send the city a day, of `normal` pieces a day for the whole group (0 pieces: no cap; a supply of 0 sends none); `price`, what the group's goods cost, both the shops' draws from the store room and the shops' prices to residents (the residents weigh nourishment for the price, so they buy what is in season); `shelf`, how full the shops keep their shelves of the group's goods (a maker stocking up ahead of a lean season). Goods made of a group's goods sit in it when their price should follow it (bread with the grain). The numbers are placeholders, each world's to change in the DM (its Economy tab) or Atlas's Economy page; `normal` is about what the city drew a day without a cap (build 48).

groups.name: grain and flour
groups.about: Harvested late summer into autumn: plentiful and cheap then, so more bread; dearer and short in winter and spring until the next harvest.

groups.name: fresh fruit
groups.about: Apples, berries and grapes: plentiful from high summer to the autumn's end, scarce in winter.

groups.name: fresh fish
groups.about: More fresh fish in winter (the user's call, 2026-10-31): the cold months' catch.

groups.name: livestock and meat
groups.about: Kept the year round: no season.

groups.name: milk and dairy
groups.about: The year round, a little less (and dearer) in winter.

groups.name: honey
groups.about: Taken from summer into autumn; scarcer in winter and spring.

groups.name: dried and preserved fruit
groups.about: The preserver's goods keep for months and don't follow the season themselves: their makers stock up in autumn, while fruit is cheap and plentiful (their shelves run to 2.5 times their sales), so there is more of them through the winter, when fresh fruit is scarce (their shelves fall back to normal by spring, so the stock is sold down before more is made). Since doc 68's follow-ups ("winter preserves"): the Country's own stores (`stores`) send them when fresh fruit runs short, a preserver that can't make them for the fruit's cap drawing them itself (at most `normal` pieces a day times `supply`: most in winter, little in summer), and they are a tenth cheaper in winter, so residents eat more of them then, beside the winter's fresh fish.
